newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Peters defiant after cleared of contempt.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters defiant after cleared of contempt.

text.p: New Zealand's Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters defiantly declined to apologise to parliament on Thursday after a privileges committee report into an alleged assault by him on a fellow MP.

In a forceful speech during a debate into the panel's findings, he said the committee, which on Wednesday cleared him of contempt, had been wrong to say he had committed an assault as it had not formed such a charge.
"Had there been a charge formulated and I got a fair hearing on that, and if then I was found guilty, I would apologise. I was not, and therefore I will not," he told a packed house.
The committee had been asked by an opposition MP to look into a late-night fracas when Peters challenged backbench MP John Banks in a corridor of the parliament building after a key debate on tax.
The panel ruled there was insufficient evidence linking the argument to parliamentary matters to find Peters in contempt.
However, it said its members believed Peters had assaulted Banks and therefore suggested he apologise to the house for what it called "unbecoming" and "unacceptable" behaviour.
The New Zealand First leader and trained lawyer challenged parliament's grounds for declaring him to have committed an assault at all.
"Was there any so-called evidence with respect to that charge? No. Was any witness called to give evidence on that charge? No," he said.

"I will never be part of this dangerous precedent whereby some unformed charge is heard by a committee and the member is never given a chance to defend himself on that charge and then he's expected to apologise," he said.

Peters, clearly aware that both the report and Thursday's debate had given opponents of the coalition government an ideal opportunity to sling mud at him and his party, said their "vile and bile" would not get them anywhere.
He reserved his harshest words for Jim Anderton, leader of the left-wing Alliance grouping, who had made the complaint to the committee after witnessing the exchange between Peters and Banks.
Peters questioned Anderton's evidence to the committee, noting he had not been able to say if Banks was punched on the shoulder, the lapel or the forearm "and he could not remember".
"You can come here and make all the trivial, petty comments you like but this is a matter of justice.
"If you think I am going to kow in front of this house while you make false statements, then you are so wrong... so wrong."
At the end of a 2-1/2 hour debate, legislators carried a motion to accept the commitee's findings.
Amendments proposed by leaders of two opposition parties to overturn the report's main conclusion, and to refer the alleged assault to a police authorities, were rejected by MPs.
Peters said he was minded to sue the author of the latter amendment, Labour Party deputy leader Michael Cullen.
